title: A chaotic invariant set in the loss-modulated class-B laser: a computer-assisted proof
description:
In plain words. In 1982 a group in Florence drove a CO2 laser into chaos by periodically wobbling how much light leaks out of it. Lasers of this kind are described by two equations, which a 2025 review studies by simulation. As far as we could find, nobody had proved that these equations have chaotic dynamics. This archive proves it at the review's own parameters: inside the laser's possible states there is a set of motions that is provably chaotic. In our long simulations at the same settings, every starting point we tried settles into a regular rhythm that repeats every 16 wobbles. So the proved chaos coexists with that rhythm; the rhythm is a numerical observation, not part of the theorem.

The idea in one picture. kneading dough. A baker stretches the dough long, lays it back across itself and stretches it again. Here the dough is the set of possible laser states, and one wobble of the losses moves it. We picked 24 small, thin boxes of states and proved that one wobble stretches each box right across the next one. Where the picture breaks. a baker mixes all the dough; in this laser our simulations show nearly the opposite, with every starting point we tried settling onto the regular rhythm. The chaos is real but hidden.

For specialists. The class-B laser rate equations with modulated losses (Oppo 2025, arXiv:2510.18472, Eq. 27), a two-variable description of loss-modulated lasers such as the 1982 Florence CO2 laser, have no rigorous chaos proof that we could find; their chaos rests on simulations. At the review's own parameters (mu = 2, eps = 0.04, omega = 1.1, m = 0.0608) we prove, with rigorous interval-arithmetic integration (CAPD), 25 covering relations for the once-per-modulation map on 24 disjoint sets built along a period-6 saddle orbit and a homoclinic excursion. Hence the map has a compact invariant chaotic set: it carries infinitely many periodic orbits and topological entropy at least 0.0537 per modulation period, and P24 has a full two-symbol shift on part of it. Numerically (not proved), the long-run motion at these parameters is a stable period-16 cycle in the last steps of the period-doubling cascade, so the proved chaos coexists with a periodic attractor. Two independently written checkers, positive and negative controls, review-seat cross-checks and a one-command reproduction are included. Text and figures CC BY 4.0; code MIT.

Links. Repository, with a plain-language guide: github.com/Hashirama1337s/laser-chaos. All projects: the Moki & Julio lab map.

Open doors. Every long simulation at the review's settings settles onto a cycle that repeats every 16 wobbles; proving that this cycle exists and attracts would settle the long-run behaviour there (an untested observation, not proved). A sweep of the wobble depth suggests lasting chaos begins between m = 0.0606 and m = 0.0610, after cycles of period 8, 16 and 32 at m = 0.0607, 0.0608 and 0.0609; where the period-doubling cascade ends exactly was not pinned down (untested observation). At the review's second chaotic example (ω = 0.47, m = 0.080) a short Lyapunov estimate is clearly negative, and at its Fig. 14(a, b) settings a larger period-3 orbit coexists; neither was followed up (untested observations). The saddle cycle and returning loop that guided the proof boxes were found by simulation only; a proof that they exist was not attempted (untested observation).

Prepared with AI assistance; what was checked, and by what, is stated above.
